title: AI-authored contributions to our codebases
content:
mySociety has had a longstanding mission to help avoid the reinvention of the wheel in civic tech. That’s why most of our code is open source, and that’s what has allowed people to run instances of sites like FixMyStreet, WhatDoTheyKnow and TheyWorkForYou in their own jurisdictions, without having to write code or manage challenges, such as those we mentioned in our previous post, themselves.

So perhaps, rather than hearing about your whole new website, we’d prefer to see you submit some AI-authored code to our existing open source codebases? 

Well, we do — with some caveats — welcome submissions to improve our services. In this brave new world where those submissions may have been created entirely, or with the help of, AI, here are the things to bear in mind:

title: So you’ve vibe coded a website and you’d like us to take a look
content:
AI tools that allow people without coding skills to spin up a website are now commonplace, and this has resulted in a rapid rise in people getting in touch with us here at mySociety. These days, a large number of the emails we’re receiving begin something like: “Hey, I’ve created this website…”

While it’s not always explicitly mentioned, it’s pretty clear the vast majority of these sites have been vibe coded — that is, written entirely by AI, most likely based only on descriptions of the intended output, and almost always without any human review or even understanding of the underlying code.

We love to hear from the civic tech community, and of course we have a keen interest in technology that makes democracy more accessible. As AI is lowering the bar to folk making a tool they’ve imagined into a reality, new projects are launching thick and fast. We’d be foolish to ignore that.

But that said, we are getting a lot of emails.

title: Developed for the public sector and kept public: explaining open source licensing
content:
We’ve copied this post from the blog of mySociety’s commercial subsidiary SocietyWorks. It’s part 2 in their Responsible Tech series, in which they explore open source technology and data privacy, security, and sovereignty. In this update, Chloe Carrington Dunn explains what open source licensing is, how to spot it and what public sector decision-makers need to know about it.

— 

The first post in this series explored the benefits of open and reusable source code. Angela Dixon, our Managing Director, made the case that “if it is the product of public spend, then it should be built to be reused and shared” and busted some of the myths around open source being more vulnerable to maleficent actors or less secure. 

If you didn’t read that first post, the tl;dr was this: publishing open source code can reduce risk, prevent vendor lock-in, and means the benefits of the code can be shared among other public sector entities. 

But not everyone understands what open source means and how to recognise when something is open source. In this blog post, I’ll clear up when open source code is used, what it means to be open, and what this means for the public sector.
